title: The American Revolution
in30Seconds: The American Revolution was the conflict in which thirteen British colonies broke from Britain and founded the United States. After the costly French and Indian War, Britain taxed the colonies without their consent, protest escalated from the Boston Massacre to the Boston Tea Party, and fighting began at Lexington and Concord in 1775. Congress declared independence on July 4, 1776; the war ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783.
whyItMatters: The Revolution created the United States and gave the modern world an influential statement of natural rights and government by consent. Understanding it lets you read the founding documents critically rather than as slogans: you can trace how a tax dispute became a claim about human equality, and how that claim was applied unevenly. It also sharpens a core historical skill, separating what happened and when from why it mattered, and holding the Revolution's ideals and its exclusions in view at the same time. Almost every later argument about American citizenship, rights, and rebellion begins here.
learningObjectives: Explain how British war debt and post-1763 taxation led to the grievance of 'no taxation without representation.'
Sequence the key events from the Stamp Act (1765) through the Treaty of Paris (1783) with accurate dates.
Distinguish the Revolution's stated ideals from how it was experienced by enslaved people, women, Native Americans, and loyalists.
Analyze why Saratoga and the French alliance were turning points in the war.
Apply the concept of 'consent of the governed' to a primary-source grievance.

collegeVersion.heading: Causes: war debt, taxes, and the rights of British subjects
collegeVersion.body: The Revolution grew out of victory, not defeat. Britain won the Seven Years' War, known in North America as the French and Indian War, which ended in 1763 and left Britain dominant but deeply in debt. To help pay for defending and administering a larger empire, Parliament began raising revenue from the colonies: the Sugar Act of 1764, then the Stamp Act of 1765, a direct tax on printed materials. Colonists reacted sharply. Many accepted that Parliament could regulate trade but insisted it could not tax them internally, because they elected no members to it. Out of this came the slogan 'no taxation without representation.' The Townshend Acts of 1767 taxed imported goods and provoked boycotts and renewed protest. The dispute was not, at first, about leaving the empire. Colonists framed their case as a defense of the ordinary rights of British subjects, arguing that a subject could be taxed only with the consent of his elected representatives. Enlightenment ideas about natural rights and government resting on the consent of the governed gave this grievance a broader, more radical vocabulary.

collegeVersion.heading: From protest to rupture: Massacre, Tea Party, and Lexington
collegeVersion.body: Protest hardened into confrontation. British troops stationed in Boston clashed with a crowd, and the conflict turned deadly on March 5, 1770, in the killing that came to be called the Boston Massacre. Tensions eased briefly, then flared again over tea. The Tea Act of 1773 lowered the price of British East India Company tea but kept a tax colonists rejected on principle. On December 16, 1773, protesters boarded ships in Boston Harbor and destroyed the cargo in what became known as the Boston Tea Party. Parliament answered in early 1774 with the Coercive Acts, called the Intolerable Acts in the colonies, which closed the port of Boston and restricted Massachusetts self-government. These measures pushed the colonies toward common action. On April 19, 1775, British regulars marching to seize colonial military stores met militia at Lexington and Concord, and the first shots of the war were fired. Armed rebellion had begun more than a year before the colonies formally declared independence.

collegeVersion.heading: Independence and the ideas behind it
collegeVersion.body: As fighting spread, the Continental Congress moved from resistance toward separation. Richard Henry Lee introduced a motion for independence on June 7, 1776, and Congress assigned the drafting of a formal declaration to a committee, with Thomas Jefferson as principal author; Benjamin Franklin and John Adams reviewed his draft. Congress adopted the final text on July 4, 1776. The Declaration of Independence did two things at once. It listed specific grievances against the king to justify the break, and it grounded the right to rebel in a general principle: 'that all men are created equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights,' and that governments derive 'their just powers from the consent of the governed.' That second move mattered far beyond 1776. By stating the case for independence as a claim about universal human rights and consent, the Declaration created a standard that later generations, including abolitionists and suffragists, would use to measure the nation against its own words.

collegeVersion.heading: The war's course and the Treaty of Paris
collegeVersion.body: The military struggle lasted eight years. Early campaigns went badly for the Continental Army under George Washington, but a major turning point came at Saratoga in New York, where the British general Burgoyne surrendered about five thousand soldiers on October 17, 1777. That victory convinced France, long hostile to Britain, that the American cause could succeed. France signed a Treaty of Alliance and a Treaty of Amity and Commerce with the United States on February 6, 1778, bringing money, troops, and a navy into the war and turning a colonial rebellion into a wider conflict. The decisive campaign came in 1781, when combined American and French forces trapped Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia; he surrendered on October 19, 1781. Fighting wound down, and negotiators signed the Treaty of Paris on September 3, 1783, in which Britain recognized the independence of the United States. A war that began as a tax dispute ended with a new nation on the map.

collegeVersion.heading: Contradictions and limits
collegeVersion.body: The Revolution's ideals and its practice did not match, and honest history holds both in view. The Declaration proclaimed that all men are created equal, yet slavery continued in the new nation, and several of the men who signed the document enslaved people themselves. For the roughly one-fifth of the population who were enslaved, revolutionary liberty was a promise withheld; some sought freedom by joining whichever side offered it. Native American nations faced a different calculation: many allied with Britain, correctly fearing that an independent United States would expand westward onto their lands, and they were among the Revolution's clear losers. Women contributed to boycotts, war production, and the home front but gained no formal political rights. Loyalists, colonists who stayed loyal to the crown, were roughly a fifth of the population; many were harassed, dispossessed, or forced into exile. Recognizing these limits does not diminish the Revolution's importance. It explains why the struggle to make 'all men are created equal' real has continued long after 1783.

vocabulary.definition: The North American theater of the Seven Years' War, ending in 1763, whose costs left Britain in debt and motivated new colonial taxes.
The colonial argument that Parliament could not tax colonists who elected none of its members and had not consented to the tax.
A 1765 British law placing a direct tax on printed materials in the colonies; its repeal followed widespread protest.
The March 5, 1770 killing of colonists by British soldiers during a street confrontation in Boston.
The December 16, 1773 destruction of British East India Company tea in Boston Harbor in protest of the Tea Act.
The 1774 British laws punishing Massachusetts, including closing Boston's port, which pushed the colonies toward united resistance.
The document adopted July 4, 1776, drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson, announcing the colonies' separation from Britain and its justifying principles.
The principle that a government's legitimate authority derives from the agreement of the people it rules.
Colonists who remained loyal to the British crown during the Revolution; many were dispossessed or exiled.
The September 3, 1783 agreement in which Britain recognized the independence of the United States and ended the war.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Britain had just fought an expensive war and wanted the colonies to help pay for it, so it added taxes. The colonists were angry not mainly because the taxes were large but because nobody had asked them, and they had no one speaking for them in the government that made the rules. Small protests grew into big ones, then into fighting. The colonists decided they would rather run their own country, so they wrote the Declaration of Independence saying people have rights no ruler can take away. After eight years of war, and help from France, they won and became the United States. But the same leaders who wrote that everyone is equal still allowed slavery and left many people out, which is a real part of the story too.
eli10.analogy: Imagine a landlord who keeps adding fees to your rent and changing the house rules, but never lets you into the meeting where those rules are decided. Eventually the tenants stop paying, hold their own meeting, and declare they are moving out to start a household of their own.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy captures the anger about being ruled without a voice, but it undersells the stakes and the unfairness inside the new household. Leaving a landlord is peaceful; the Revolution was an eight-year war that killed thousands. And the tenants who 'started their own household' did not extend their new freedom to everyone under their roof, since slavery continued and many people were excluded.

workedExample: Read one grievance from the Declaration: the colonists accuse the king of 'imposing Taxes on us without our Consent.' Work through why this line matters. First, identify the principle behind it, that legitimate authority rests on the consent of the governed. Second, connect it to the earlier fight over the Stamp Act (1765) and Townshend Acts (1767), where colonists objected not to the amount of the tax but to being taxed by a Parliament they did not elect. Third, notice what the grievance does rhetorically: it reframes a specific policy dispute as a violation of a universal right, which justifies not just protest but separation. Finally, test the principle against the Revolution's own record. If consent is the standard, then enslaved people, women, and Native American nations were governed without their consent by the very republic that made the argument, which is exactly the tension later reformers pressed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking the colonists rebelled because taxes were unusually high.
commonMistakes.correction: The core objection was constitutional, not financial: they held that Parliament could not tax them without their consent because they elected no representatives to it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating July 4, 1776 as the day the war was won or the day fighting started.
commonMistakes.correction: Fighting began at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775; July 4, 1776 is when Congress adopted the Declaration. The war continued until 1783.
A large minority were loyalists who backed the crown, and many colonists were neutral; the population was divided, not unanimous.

commonMistakes.mistake: Presenting 'all men are created equal' as an accomplished fact of the new nation.
commonMistakes.correction: It was a stated ideal contradicted in practice by slavery and by the exclusion of women and Native Americans; the gap between ideal and reality is central to the history.

commonMistakes.mistake: Crediting the American victory to the colonists alone.
commonMistakes.correction: The French alliance of 1778, prompted by Saratoga, brought decisive money, troops, and naval power, seen most clearly at Yorktown in 1781.

compareContrast.distinction: The Massacre was a deadly street clash that produced martyrs and propaganda; the Tea Party was an organized, deliberate destruction of property to protest the Tea Act. One was violence against people, the other targeted goods.

Lee's motion for independence was introduced June 7 and approved before the wording was finished; July 4 is the date Congress adopted the final text, which is why it appears on the document and became the holiday.
Saratoga was the turning point that brought France into the war; Yorktown was the decisive final campaign that made British continuation untenable and led to peace.

keyTakeaway: The American Revolution turned a dispute over taxation without consent into a war for independence and a lasting claim that governments rest on the consent of the governed, a claim the new nation proclaimed while denying it to the enslaved, to women, and to Native peoples.

questionBank.prompt: On what date did the confrontation known as the Boston Massacre take place?
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax states conflict 'turned deadly on March 5, 1770.' December 16, 1773 is the Boston Tea Party, April 19, 1775 is Lexington and Concord, and July 4, 1776 is the adoption of the Declaration.
questionBank.skill: Recall of a key date in the imperial crisis

questionBank.prompt: Which battle is generally identified as the turning point that helped bring France into the war as a formal ally?
questionBank.explanation: The British surrender at Saratoga on October 17, 1777 convinced France to sign a formal alliance on February 6, 1778. Yorktown (1781) was the decisive final campaign, and Lexington and Concord opened the war.
questionBank.skill: Identifying the strategic significance of Saratoga

questionBank.prompt: A student notes that colonists protested the Stamp Act even though it was a relatively small tax. Which reasoning best explains their objection?
options: They believed all taxation was inherently illegal under British law.
They wanted to break from Britain immediately and needed a pretext.
They objected only because the tax fell on tea and other luxuries.
They held that Parliament could not tax them without their consent, since they elected no members to it.
questionBank.explanation: The grievance was constitutional: 'no taxation without representation.' Colonists accepted trade regulation but denied that a Parliament they did not elect could tax them. They were not yet seeking independence, did not reject all taxation, and the Stamp Act taxed printed materials, not tea.
questionBank.skill: Explaining the constitutional basis of colonial protest

questionBank.prompt: Who was the principal drafter of the Declaration of Independence, and when did Congress adopt its final text?
questionBank.explanation: Congress assigned the drafting to Thomas Jefferson, whose draft Franklin and Adams reviewed, and adopted the final text on July 4, 1776. Lee introduced the motion for independence on June 7; September 3, 1783 is the Treaty of Paris.
questionBank.skill: Attributing authorship and dating the Declaration

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best captures a central contradiction of the American Revolution?
options: It declared independence but never actually separated from Britain.
It proclaimed that 'all men are created equal' while slavery continued and women and Native Americans were excluded from its new freedoms.
It was won without any foreign assistance despite claims to the contrary.
It abolished slavery immediately but denied the vote to landowners.
questionBank.explanation: The Declaration's claim of universal equality coexisted with the continuation of slavery and the exclusion of women, Native Americans, and others. The colonies did separate from Britain, France's aid was decisive, and slavery was not abolished by the Revolution.
questionBank.skill: Evaluating the gap between the Revolution's ideals and its practice
